The ANT models

ANT-4B and ANT-08B are open-source System 1 decision models. Give one a state, a question and a list of candidates, and it answers with calibrated probabilities and a verdict: act on the top candidate, or hand the decision back.

Which department should handle this case?

Customer has been charged twice for the same invoice. Refund requested.

  • Billing team 43.9%
  • Engineering support 36.0%
  • CS team 8.0%
  • Sales team 6.4%
  • InfoSec 3.4%
  • Counsel 2.3%
Billing team escalate

The label matches, but the margin over engineering support is too narrow to act on, so the policy hands it back.

The models

Same recipe, two backbones. Both heads were trained on the same multitask dataset for the same three epochs, with the same batch size, learning rate and seed, so the numbers below compare backbones rather than training runs.

What both models share

  • A frozen Qwen backbone used as an encoder. No LM head, no text generation.
  • 5,952 training rows, 688 validation, 648 test, 456 out-of-distribution.
  • 29 use cases, in English and Italian.
  • Two to a hundred candidates, order does not matter, embeddings cache.
  • Apache-2.0, and work in progress on both repositories.

ANT-4B The model that holds on the hard cases

ANT-4B freezes a Qwen3.5-4B decoder and turns it into an encoder, then learns a 2.6-million-parameter scoring head on top of it. It is the larger of the two models, and on the same test split it is the one that keeps its accuracy where fine semantic discrimination is needed.

Ranking, not writing. Give ANT-4B a state, a question and any number of candidates, and it returns a calibrated probability for each one, plus a verdict: act on the top candidate, or escalate. The candidate order does not change the probabilities, and a candidate set can be embedded once and reused across follow-up questions.

ANT-08B The same recipe on a smaller backbone

ANT-08B runs the same training recipe as ANT-4B on a frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B: same data, same three epochs, same seed, so the comparison between them is between backbones and not between runs. It is competitive on routing and classification, and it is the one that fits on a laptop.

The lightweight twin. ANT-08B scores the same candidate sets with a 1-million-parameter head, and it wins on several use cases where meaning is coarse: order intent, document type, lead quality, meeting action. It loses where the distinction is fine, and its calibration degrades faster outside the training distribution.

Where they still fail

  • transaction_risk is near chance for both models: 0.125 for the 4B and 0.000 for the 0.8B, on eight test rows.
  • urgenza_ticket_it sits around 0.35 for both. More parameters will not fix those two; they are first on the list for the next data pass.
  • Both repositories are marked work in progress on purpose: the benchmarks and the calibration guidance are not finished.

How a decision is made

ANT does not generate text. The decoder behind it is used as an encoder, the trainable part is a small scoring head, and the output is meant for software that has to act.

Encode the state and every candidate.

One shared frozen decoder embeds the state with its question, and each candidate separately.

Score them in a single pass.

One logit per candidate, then a softmax with a fitted temperature turns the logits into probabilities.

Decide, or hand it back.

A risk and coverage policy fitted on validation data decides whether the top probability is good enough to act on.

Encoding: one frozen decoder, two encoders. Full size in the build log 

result = ant.predict(
    state,
    question,
    candidates=[
        "Billing",
        "Technical Support",
        "Sales",
        "Legal",
    ],
)

What comes back

The chosen candidate, the calibrated probability of every candidate, the confidence metrics and the action: execute or escalate.

Thirteen seconds to 372 milliseconds

The first working prediction on the 4B model took about thirteen seconds on the M3, which made the playground unusable. Encoding dominated the profile, and the path was doing it twice: one fused single-pass encode, inference mode and length bucketing brought the warm median to 372 ms on a fourteen-token input, about eight times faster. Longer inputs still cost — 1,446 ms at 210 tokens, 2,866 ms at 418 — and the floor is the linear attention, not the tuning.

Try it

The playground is a FastAPI server plus a Vite interface. Point it at one or more checkpoint directories and it lists the models it can serve; every request runs through the same predictor the Python API uses.
